posts.headline: American households now owe $19.1 trillion
posts.source: Source: New York Fed, Q3 2026 Household Debt and Credit Report
posts.caption:
Household debt grew by $334 billion in just three months.

That is the New York Fed's count for July to September 2026, released this week. Total debt is now $19.1 trillion, up 1.8% in the quarter.

Most of the rise was mortgages and home equity lines. The share of all debt in some stage of delinquency rose to 5.0%, from 4.7% the quarter before.

My take: the total grabs the headline, but the late-payment share is the number that tells you how households are coping.

Has your own debt gone up or down this year?

Source: New York Fed, Q3 2026 Household Debt and Credit Report (Nov 10 2026)
Educational only — not financial advice.

#HouseholdDebt #PersonalFinance #Economy

data.dek: Up $334 billion in one quarter, July to September. 5.0% of it is now behind on payments, up from 4.7%.

posts.headline: Gas fell 16 cents a gallon in one week
posts.source: Source: US Energy Information Administration, week of Nov 9 2026
posts.caption:
A full tank just got about $2.37 cheaper.

The national average for regular gas was $3.995 a gallon in the week of November 9, per the EIA. The week before it was $4.153. That is a 15.8-cent drop.

On a 15-gallon fill-up, the difference is about $2.37.

It is still well above where prices were a year ago.

My take: one good week does not undo a year of higher prices, but it is real money for anyone who drives to work.

Have you noticed it at your pump yet?

Source: US Energy Information Administration, weekly retail gasoline prices, week of Nov 9 2026
Educational only — not financial advice.

#GasPrices #CostOfLiving #Energy

posts.headline: Shoppers kept spending in October, but only just
posts.caption:
Retail spending grew at its slowest monthly pace in nearly a year.

Shoppers spent $561.7 billion in October, seasonally adjusted, per the CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor. That is up just 0.2% from September, the smallest monthly gain since November 2025. Against October 2025 it is up 3.6%.

The NRF says Halloween and early holiday deals kept it from slowing more.

My take: people are still buying, but they are waiting for the sale first. That is what a stretched budget looks like.

Are you holding off on anything until a deal shows up?

Source: CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor, October 2026
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: How buy now, pay later really works
posts.caption:
Pay in four sounds simple. Here is the part the checkout page skips.

Most plans split the price into four payments. The first is due at checkout, the rest every two weeks.

Pay on time and many plans charge no interest. Miss one and a late fee can apply, and some providers may report it to the credit bureaus.

The real risk is stacking: three small plans can mean three payments in one week.

My take: it is a payment schedule, not extra money. Treat it like a bill the day you click.

How many plans could you have running by New Year?

Source: Follow the Money explainer — terms vary by provider
Educational only — not financial advice.

posts.headline: Credit card debt just hit a record
posts.source: Source: New York Fed, Q3 2026 Household Debt and Credit Report
posts.caption:
Americans now carry $1.29 trillion on credit cards, the highest on record.

Balances rose $22 billion from July to September 2026, per the New York Fed. They are up 4.2% from a year earlier.

One bright spot: new card delinquencies improved slightly. Student loans went the other way, with 10.9% of balances now 90+ days late.

My take: a record balance is not a crisis on its own. A record balance at today's card rates is expensive for whoever carries it.

Is your card balance higher or lower than this time last year?

Source: New York Fed, Q3 2026 Household Debt and Credit Report (Nov 10 2026)
Educational only — not financial advice.

#CreditCards #Debt #PersonalFinance

data.footnote: Balances as of end of September 2026 (Q3). Student loan figure is the share of balances seriously delinquent.

posts.headline: 15 years or 30 years: the interest gap is huge
posts.caption:
Same house, same rate. One loan costs almost $192,000 more in interest.

Borrow $300,000 at 6% fixed. Over 30 years the payment is about $1,799 a month, and you pay about $347,500 in interest.

Over 15 years the payment is about $2,532, but total interest is about $155,700.

That is about $733 more a month, in exchange for roughly $191,800 less interest.

My take: the right term depends on the monthly payment you can carry, not just the total. But it helps to know the total.

Which would you choose, and why?

Source: standard amortization math, $300,000 at 6% fixed, principal and interest only
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Mortgages #HomeBuying #MoneyMath

posts.headline: Myth: carrying a card balance builds your credit
posts.caption:
This one costs people real interest every month.

Fact: you do not need to carry a balance to build credit. Using the card and paying the statement in full on time builds your payment history just the same.

What a balance does do is charge you interest. And a high balance compared with your limit can actually weigh on your score.

My take: the bank is happy for this myth to live forever. It is one of the most profitable misunderstandings in personal finance.

Who told you this one first?

Source: Follow the Money explainer
Educational only — not financial advice.

#CreditScore #CreditCards #MoneyMyths

posts.headline: $1 million today, or a penny doubled for 30 days?
posts.caption:
Most people take the million. Most people would be wrong.

Start with one cent and double it every day. On day 20 you have about $5,243. On day 25, about $167,772. Still looks like a bad deal.

Then day 29: $2.68 million. Day 30: $5.37 million.

Nearly all of the growth happens at the very end. That is how compounding works, and why it is so easy to give up on early.

My take: real money does not double daily, but the shape of the curve is exactly the same.

Which would you have picked?

Source: calculated, $0.01 doubled each day for 30 days
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Compounding #MoneyMath #WouldYouRather

posts.headline: What a fund fee quietly takes from you
posts.source: Source: calculated, 6% a year before fees
posts.caption:
A 1% fee sounds small. Over 30 years it is not.

Put $100,000 in an investment earning 6% a year before fees and leave it for 30 years.

With a 0.1% yearly fee you end up with about $558,000. With 0.5%, about $498,000. With 1%, about $432,000.

That is roughly $126,000 lost to the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive.

My take: you cannot control returns. You can see the fee, and it is charged every single year.

Do you know what your 401(k) or IRA funds charge?

Source: calculated, $100,000 at 6% a year before fees, 30 years
Educational only — not financial advice.

#Investing #RetirementSavings #Fees

data.footnote: $100,000 growing at 6% a year before fees for 30 years, nothing added. Illustration, not a forecast.

posts.headline: What a 3% raise every year adds up to
posts.caption:
A 3% raise feels like nothing in the year you get it.

Start at $50,000 and get 3% every year. After 10 years you earn about $67,200. After 20, about $90,300. After 30, about $121,400.

Each raise is built on top of the last one. That is why your first salary negotiation matters for decades.

These are before inflation. If prices rise 3% a year too, your buying power stays about where it started.

My take: a raise only counts if it beats prices. Check yours against inflation, not against zero.

Did your last raise keep up?

Source: calculated, $50,000 salary with 3% yearly raises, before inflation
